results.title: Determine which CUDA is in use in a Conda environment - PyTorch Forums
results.content: # Determine which CUDA is in use in a Conda environment. You have selected **0** posts. ## post by IcarusWizard on Feb 21, 2024. I am a big fan of Conda and always use it to create virtual environments for my experiments since it can manage different versions of CUDA easily. Normally, I will install PyTorch with the recommended conda way, e.g. `conda install pytorch torchvision torchaudio pytorch-cuda=11.8 -c pytorch -c nvidia`. But recently, I have some RL experiments that need to run in a docker container which is based on `nvidia/cudagl:11.4.2-devel-ubuntu20.04` that has a system-level cuda 11.4 install in it. Somehow, the conda install solution doesn’t work anymore. The `torch.cuda.is_available` always return false. However, when I try to install PyTorch with pip, it seems like it also installs some cuda-related package and make `torch.cuda.is_available` return true. If I have multiple cuda installation from different source, e.g. system-level, conda and pip, which cuda is actually in use? I see there are some post say one can use `` to check the cuda version, but I feel it always returns the version that the code is compiled with, even when `torch.cuda.is_available` returns false. ## post by ptrblck on Feb 21, 2024. The PyTorch binaries ship with their own CUDA dependencies, which are selected/specified in the install command. Your locally installed CUDA toolkit won’t be used unless you build PyTorch from source or a custom CUDA extension. ## post by IcarusWizard on Feb 21, 2024. So you mean that for the pip installation, some CUDA dependencies is installed *inside* PyTorch package, so that it never misuses other versions. But why does conda fail in this case? It should also use the CUDA it shipped with right? ## post by ptrblck on Feb 21, 2024. Yes, the pip wheels depend on the CUDA libs hosted on PyPI (e.g. `nvidia-cuda-runtime-cu12`, `nvidia-cudnn-cu12`, etc.) while the conda binaries use their corresponding packages from the `nvidia` conda channel. I don’t know why the conda binaries do not work inside your container, but outside they seem to work. ### New & Unread Topics. Topic list, column headers with buttons are sortable. results.title: Pytorch does not detect CUDA when used within miniconda docker - deployment - PyTorch Forums
results.content: # Pytorch does not detect CUDA when used within miniconda docker. The pytorch run within the container cannot detect the CUDA libs when using the miniconda base image. $ conda install pytorch torchvision torchaudio cudatoolkit=10.2 -c pytorch. CUDA runtime version: Could not collect. [conda] pytorch 1.11.0 py3.9_cuda10.2_cudnn7.6.5_0 pytorch. [conda] pytorch-mutex 1.0 cuda pytorch. | NVIDIA-SMI 470.57.02 Driver Version: 470.57.02 CUDA Version: 11.4 |. `nvidia-smi` result within the container shows CUDA version as NA. | NVIDIA-SMI 470.57.02 Driver Version: 470.57.02 CUDA Version: N/A |. On the other hand, if I use the official docker image `nvidia/cuda` and install conda and pytorch following the same step as above, it can be used normally. CUDA runtime version: Could not collect. [conda] pytorch 1.11.0 py3.9_cuda10.2_cudnn7.6.5_0 pytorch. [conda] pytorch-mutex 1.0 cuda pytorch`. `nvidia-smi` result when run within the container can detect the CUDA version. But my understanding is that `pytorch` only requires a valid nvidia driver when installed using `conda`. `conda` will install `cudatoolkit` and `cudnn` along `pytorch`.

results.content: All content displayed below is AI generate content. ## What are the best practices for managing CUDA and cuDNN versions in a high-performance computing environment? Managing CUDA and cuDNN versions effectively is critical for maintaining stability, performance, and compatibility in high-performance computing (HPC) environments. Proper version control ensures seamless operation across GPU-accelerated workloads, machine learning frameworks, and scientific computing applications. ### Understand Compatibility Requirements Before installing or upgrading CUDA and cuDNN, verify compatibility with your hardware and software stack. NVIDIA GPUs have specific CUDA architecture support, and frameworks like TensorFlow or PyTorch require particular CUDA and cuDNN versions. Always consult NVIDIA's documentation and framework release notes. ### Use Containerization for Isolation Containers (e.g., Docker, Singularity) simplify version management by encapsulating CUDA, cuDNN, and application dependencies. * **Reproducibility:** Ensures consistent environments across different systems. * **Isolation:** Prevents conflicts between different CUDA/cuDNN versions. * **Portability:** Easily deploy GPU-accelerated workloads across clusters or cloud platforms. ### Leverage NVIDIA's NGC Containers NVIDIA NGC provides pre-configured containers optimized for HPC and AI workloads. * Tested CUDA and cuDNN versions. * Popular frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch) with GPU acceleration. * Regular updates for performance and security. ### Implement Version Pinning Explicitly specify CUDA and cuDNN versions in your environment setup to avoid unexpected updates. * Using *conda* environments with version-locked packages. * Setting environment variables (e.g., *CUDA\_HOME*, *LD\_LIBRARY\_PATH*). ### Maintain a Version Matrix Document supported CUDA, cuDNN, and driver versions for your applications. A version matrix helps teams: * Plan upgrades without disrupting workflows. ### Automate Testing and Validation Automated CI/CD pipelines should validate CUDA and cuDNN compatibility before deployment. * Running unit tests with different CUDA versions. ### Monitor Driver and Toolkit Updates NVIDIA frequently releases updates for CUDA toolkits and GPU drivers. * Testing new versions in staging environments before production. ### Use System-Level Management Tools Tools like *Environment Modules* or *Spack* help manage multiple CUDA versions on shared HPC systems. * Switch between CUDA versions dynamically. * Load specific cuDNN libraries as needed. * Maintain clean separation between environments. By following these best practices, organizations can optimize GPU performance, minimize compatibility issues, and streamline workflows in high-performance computing environments. ### Need GPU Compute?
